amendments.rule: Where a Greek adjective and an expressed Greek noun are both anarthrous and the ASV supplies a determiner for the phrase, the determiner belongs to the **noun**, and any supplied case preposition goes with it. `Ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτου χρόνου` → *In the last time* gives *last* to the adjective and the discontinuous *the … time* to the noun, as `ὥραν … ἑβδόμην` → *at the seventh hour* gives *seventh* to the ordinal and *at the … hour* to the noun, and `μόνῳ θεῷ` → *to the only God* gives *only* to the adjective and *to the … God* to the noun. Rule 15 is what permits the discontinuity, and rule 51's *the word it determines* is what chooses the noun: a determiner determines the noun phrase, and an attributive adjective is only a modifier inside it. Rule 22 and rule 49 are the contrast, and the test is the one rules 31 and 47 already use — whether a head noun is expressed. Where the adjective is substantival it **is** the nominal word and takes the determiner itself, so `νεκρῶν` → *the dead*, `τυφλῶν` → *of the blind* and `ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδάμ` → *the seventh from Adam* are its own; and where a Greek article is present, rules 19 and 21 give it the determiner instead, so `τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεόν` → *the only true God* gives *the* to the article and a bare *only* to the adjective. Do not read a supplied determiner off English word order merely because it stands next to the adjective. A supplied generic **noun** is decided the same way and by the same test, this rule's reasoning reaching it unchanged: a supplied nominal completes the noun phrase, and an attributive adjective is only a modifier inside it. So where the ASV supplies a nominal for such a phrase — commonly because it has recast the expressed Greek noun as an English verb — that nominal belongs to the **expressed noun**, and the adjective keeps only the words that render it. `κριτηρίων ἐλαχίστων` → *to judge the smallest matters* gives the discontinuous *to judge the … matters* to the noun and a bare *smallest* to the adjective, and `βιωτικὰ … κριτήρια` → *to judge things pertaining to this life* gives *to judge things* to the noun and *pertaining to this life* to the adjective, the ASV's own gloss notes there — *Greek of the smallest tribunals*, *Greek tribunals pertaining to* — showing which English word answers to which token. Rule 66 then heads such a unit on whichever of the noun's English words glosses the lexeme and not on the supplied generic one, which is why both of those head on *judge*. Rule 17's generic-noun clause is not the contrast, being scoped in terms to a **substantival** adjective or demonstrative, where no noun stands to take the supplied nominal: the same `βιωτικά` standing alone → *things that pertain to this life* keeps *things* in the adjective's own unit, so a chapter writing both is following rule 24's habit and not two analyses. Rule 102 is this same principle where a Greek article governs the phrase, the article taking the supplied noun there for the same reason. Do not read a supplied nominal off English word order merely because it stands next to the adjective, and do not hand it to the adjective because the ASV renders that adjective by a phrase reading like a noun phrase elsewhere.
amendments.why: 1CO.6 split on exactly this. 6:2 and 6:4 carry the same anarthrous [attributive adjective + κριτήριον], both recast by the ASV as *to judge* plus an object noun phrase, and the verse passes put the supplied generic noun on different tokens (*matters* on the noun at 6:2, *things* on the adjective at 6:4) because the contract fixed the placement of a supplied **determiner** in this configuration and said nothing about a supplied **noun**. Rule 17's generic-noun clause is scoped to substantival adjectives, rule 102 to articular phrases, and neither reaches an anarthrous phrase whose head noun is expressed, so a verse pass had nothing to decide it with. The amendment states rule 58's own reasoning for the supplied noun, keeps the substantival contrast (6:3) explicit so the extension cannot be over-read, and points at rule 66 for the head, which is where the two corrected units already sit. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule because rule 58 is the sentence a later reader will find first, and a cross-reference would leave it silent on the case it now decides.

conventions: κριτήριον (6:2, 6:4) is recast by the ASV as the infinitival *to judge* together with a supplied generic object noun — *matters* at 6:2, *things* at 6:4 — and both English words belong to κριτήριον, headed on *judge*. The attributive adjective beside it keeps only the words that render it: *smallest* at 6:2, *pertaining to this life* at 6:4. The ASV's gloss notes ('Greek of the smallest tribunals', 'Greek tribunals pertaining to') are what map the words onto the tokens. Substantival βιωτικά at 6:3 is the contrast and keeps *things that pertain to this life* whole, no noun standing to take the supplied nominal.

The ASV's discourse-opening *Nay* is given to the strong adversative where one stands and to the inferential particle where none does: 6:8 ἀλλά takes *Nay, but* whole, headed on *but*, and 6:7 οὖν takes the bare *Nay*, the correlative μέν standing unrepresented under rule 70 in both 6:4 and 6:7. Giving 6:7's *Nay* to μέν instead remains defensible and is recorded on that unit.

report: Read all 35 candidate groups and the dump end to end. The chapter marks no unit `added` (308 aligned, 4 noncompositional, 19 unrepresented), so every supplied English word is folded and the table's blindness to `added` units hides nothing here.

One real split, at κριτήριον. 6:2 and 6:4 carry the same construction — an anarthrous attributive adjective with an expressed anarthrous κριτήριον, both recast by the ASV as *to judge* plus an object noun phrase — and put the supplied generic noun on different tokens: 6:2 gives *matters* to κριτηρίων, 6:4 gave *things* to βιωτικά. Nothing in the source licenses the difference. 6:4 is patched to match 6:2, which is the internal control and is corroborated by the ASV's own gloss at 6:4, 'Greek tribunals pertaining to', which maps *things* onto κριτήρια and *pertaining to* onto the adjective.

6:3 is deliberately untouched: there βιωτικά is substantival with no noun expressed, so it keeps *things* under rule 17's generic-noun clause. The difference between 6:3 and 6:4 is the presence of an expressed head noun, which is the test rules 22, 31, 47 and 58 already use, so it is licensed and not a second split.

Cleared as source-licensed rather than split: article before a participle (6:4 *who are of no account* under rule 90 against 6:16–18 *he that …* under rule 32 — the ASV writes one English word for the pair in the first and two in the rest); ἐάν (6:4 conditional, 6:18 generalizing with no -soever, rule 72); ἑαυτῶν (6:7 reciprocal, 6:19 reflexive possessive); the article before a noun the ASV determines (6:16 *to a harlot* aligned under rule 51 against anarthrous 6:15 *of a harlot* folding the indefinite as a helper); μέν unrepresented alike at 6:4 and 6:7; every article in 6:13 decided by whether the ASV writes a determiner, and the article before θεός emptied alike at 6:13, 6:14 and 6:20.

BSB disagreements: all five are documented convention differences and none is an error. μέν 6:7 (rule 70, no English word written); τοῦ 6:11 (rule 20, ἡμῶν takes the possessive in *our God*); εἰς 6:16 (rule 36, *shall become one flesh* realizes it nowhere); ἐάν 6:18 (rule 72); τό 6:18 (rule 47, ἴδιον carries *his own*). No accepted edge was changed to move the aggregate.

1CO.6.8 ὑμεῖς → *ye yourselves* headed on *ye* is left standing against its own note's concession to rule 107: that rule is scoped in terms to intensive αὐτός, and the corpus heads σύ → *ye yourselves* on *ye* in all four of its units, as it heads *your own* on *your* and *thine own* on *thine*. No rule is written for this, the scoping being already explicit.
One amendment: rule 58 is extended from a supplied determiner to a supplied generic noun, which is what this chapter's split turned on.
